ACT-EN2C-P1-Q01.note: "a wooden double of the part" renames "a pattern"; a nonrestrictive appositive takes a comma. The colon is the only real competitor and it fails the standard rule (Chicago 6.61) that a colon be preceded by an independent clause - the material in front of it here is the relative clause "whose bench turns out no parts, only a pattern," which cannot stand alone. The semicolon has an independent clause on neither side; bare "pattern" runs the noun into its own renaming. The superlative "most acceptable" also protects the item. FOUR-WORDS-AFTER TEST: FAILS. The next words are "a wooden double of" - a bare noun phrase in apposition, which by itself selects the comma and eliminates the semicolon and the zero-mark option. A solver who reads nothing but the four words after the blank answers this correctly. The load-bearing fact for the colon (that the preceding material is not an independent clause) lies BEFORE the blank, so the shortcut does not merely narrow the field, it lands on the key.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q02.note: "Half the patterns" takes its number from the object of the fraction, so plural; "on her rack" is the intervening prepositional phrase and supplies no subject. No recognised convention gives a singular here - notional agreement runs the other way with a plural object, and there is no collective noun to license British-style singular. Tense is settled independently: paragraph 1 is present throughout, which kills "was" twice over. FOUR-WORDS-AFTER TEST: CLEAN. After the blank comes "older than the furnace", which carries no number or tense information; every clue is upstream. That is the right construction for this family. The weakness is the option SET, not the passage: three of four options are singular and exactly one is plural, so a solver who has decided only that the subject is plural has a single survivor, and a blind solver sees an odd-one-out. Consider replacing "has been" with a plural distractor (e.g. "were") so that number and tense have to be settled separately.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q03.note: The same sentence times the cooling at "the eleven hours a heavy casting sits in its sand" and describes the metal "drawing in on itself the whole time": slow and continuous, which is what "gradually" names. No second option is defensible - "suddenly" and "quickly" contradict the eleven hours, "intermittently" contradicts "the whole time". FOUR-WORDS-AFTER TEST: PARTIAL FAIL. The four words after the blank are "over the eleven hours", which on their own destroy "suddenly" and "quickly" - two of the three distractors - leaving a coin flip between "gradually" and "intermittently". The clue that settles that last pair ("the whole time") sits nine words further on, so the shortcut narrows 4 to 2 but does not finish the item. Rated easy rather than the batch's medium: "suddenly" and "quickly" are near-synonyms of each other and die to the same clue, so the option set is effectively three-wide.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q04.pick: Yes, because it opens the distinction that paragraph 3 builds its whole account on.
ACT-EN2C-P1-Q04.note: With the source, only B survives. A credits the sentence with an "exact fraction" it plainly does not contain. C asserts paragraph 2 "has settled on one fixed fraction" - paragraph 2 names no fraction at all; the eighth-inch figure first appears in paragraph 3. D asserts the metals are "not a subject this essay returns to" - they are the subject of paragraphs 3, 4 and 5. So exclusive, and the key is right. AUTHOR'S RISK FLAG - I AGREE, AND THE ITEM IS WORSE THAN A FREE 50%. Holding all four in one frame was the right move and the two Yes / two No split does remove the crudest direction tell, but two leaks survive without the passage: (1) A is refutable against the STEM ALONE. The sentence to be added is quoted in the stem, so a blind solver can read "The fraction is not the same for every metal", see that it contains no number, and strike A with certainty - no passage needed. (2) D runs the "not a subject this essay returns to" formula, which is a scope denial about an essay the solver cannot see but whose topic the quoted sentence advertises; in a four-option add-a-sentence item that shape is almost never the key. Blind, this is a two-way choice between B and C with B favoured on shape, because C is the only remaining option that makes a checkable claim about the passage while B makes a claim about function that any relevant-looking sentence satisfies. Expect blind well above 50, consistent with the stratum's 76%. This is the CLAUDE.md axis-alignment failure in its exact form: the stem names the axis (should this be added, and why) and the options differ ALONG that axis - two of them by making claims falsifiable from the stem's own quoted sentence. The fix is not the key and not the letter: make every option's stated reason unfalsifiable without the passage. Concretely, strike the words "exact fraction" from A so it no longer self-refutes (e.g. "Yes, because paragraph 2 has been building toward it"), and replace D's essay-scope denial with a local claim about paragraph 2 that is true-sounding and only checkable in the text. SECONDARY, NOT A KEY OBJECTION: the added sentence opens with the definite "The fraction" although paragraph 2 has introduced no fraction. That is a genuine cohesion wobble in the material the key endorses, and a careful reader may notice it; it does not make any other option defensible, because no No option states that reason. Worth tightening the sentence to "That allowance is not the same for every metal."

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q05.note: "Bronze shrinks" and "aluminum shrinks nearly twice as much as gray iron does" are both independent; the comma is a splice and the zero-mark option a run-on. The colon is the only competitor worth arguing and it fails on meaning, not on form: a colon between independent clauses requires the second to explain, illustrate or amplify the first, and this second clause sets a DIFFERENT metal beside the first rather than unpacking it. So exclusive. FOUR-WORDS-AFTER TEST: FAILS OUTRIGHT, and this is the worst instance in the batch. The two words after the blank are "aluminum shrinks" - subject plus finite verb, i.e. an independent clause begins immediately. A solver who reads only that picks the semicolon and is done; nothing before the blank is needed, and even the colon is eliminated by the same reading for anyone applying the crude "two independent clauses take a semicolon" rule. Separate authoring remark: "Bronze shrinks" as a standalone clause is contentless (every metal shrinks - paragraph 3 is about how MUCH), which both weakens the prose and tempts a solver toward reading the two clauses as parallel list items. Giving the first clause a quantity would fix the prose and push the clue further from the blank.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q06.note: Three objects of "would mean": "doing the arithmetic on every dimension", "checking it against the drawing", and the blank. The first two are gerunds, so the third must be "weighing". No second option survives: "weighed" and "weighs" are finite and the series gives them no subject, and the infinitive is the error under test. No convention rescues a mixed gerund/infinitive series after a single governing verb. FOUR-WORDS-AFTER TEST: CLEAN, and this is the model item in the batch for that property. After the blank comes "a scrapped pour against", which is the same object complement under every candidate form and discriminates nothing; the whole anchor - the two prior gerunds - sits well BEFORE the blank, so the item can only be solved by reading back. Rated medium against the batch's hard: the parallel series is explicit and adjacent, and two of the three distractors fail on the same one-line objection.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q07.note: The prior sentence says what Kessel has never done (set the scheme down in a manual) and this sentence names what occupies that place (a strip of tape), so the connector marks substitution: "Instead". "In addition" would add the tape to a manual the prior sentence denies. "Still" concedes, and nothing is being conceded. CLOSEST CALL IN THE BATCH AFTER Q09, and the reason I am re-rating the difficulty: "Therefore" is not absurd. A defense can be written - the tape's status as the ONLY list is in part a consequence of no manual existing, and consequence connectives are licensed by that entailment. I still vote exclusive because the entailment is partial (the absence of a manual does not produce the tape, and "the only list" is licensed by the absence of every other record, not by the manual alone) while substitution is exact, and because the stem's "most logical" is a superlative that tolerates an inferior second reading. But the batch's difficulty label of easy is wrong: an item with a live consequence reading is not an easy item, and a solver who has not noticed that "the tape stands IN PLACE OF the manual" will land on "Therefore". Re-rate medium. If the author wants it to stay easy, weaken "Therefore" by making the tape predate the decision not to write a manual.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q08.note: EXCLUSIVITY FAILS - this is my one false vote, and I think it drops the item. The key "shop's door" is correct. But option D, bare "shop", yields "a strip of tape on the shop door", which is unimpeachable edited American English: an attributive noun modifying a head noun, the same construction as "shop floor", "barn door", "car door", "school gate". The stem asks for what is "most acceptable", and both "the shop's door" and "the shop door" are fully acceptable, refer to the same door, and carry the same meaning; nothing in the context forces the genitive. The author's explanation misstates the grammar - it rejects "shop" for "leaving the noun modifying 'door' with nothing to show ownership", but attributive nouns are not required to show ownership; that is precisely what distinguishes them from genitives. The trap backfires here because "shop" is one of the most freely compounding nouns in English, and the passage itself uses that register ("the shop floor" idiom is the exact parallel). The other two options are sound distractors - bare plural "shops" marks no possession, "shops'" invents several shops - so the item is one substitution away from working. FIX: replace "shop" with a fourth option that cannot compound, or move the possessive onto a noun that does not form a compound with its head (Bracht's, the foreman's). FOUR-WORDS-AFTER TEST: PARTIAL FAIL, and it interacts with the defect above. The single word after the blank is "door", a head noun, which on its own kills the bare plural "shops" and tells a solver that a possessive-or-attributive form is wanted. It narrows 4 to 2 without any reading, and the surviving pair is exactly the pair that is genuinely ambiguous. Number (one shop, not several) is the only thing the passage has to supply, and paragraph 5's "the shop's own allowance" supplies it - note that the passage already contains the singular possessive, so a solver can also pattern-match rather than reason.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q09.note: The next two sentences give the procedure the word has to name: Bracht takes a published figure for the nearest metal she already pours, cuts to it, waits, and then measures the first casting cold so the gap becomes the shop's own allowance. A number taken from a source and afterward corrected against measurement is an estimate. "guess" (No Change) and "hunch" both deny the figure any basis, and the paragraph supplies the basis in the very next clause. THE COMPETITOR IS "assumption", and it is the strongest wrong answer in the batch: she does assume the new alloy shrinks like its nearest neighbour, and the paragraph's test-and-revise structure is exactly what one does to an assumption. I still vote exclusive on two grounds. First, collocation: the frame is "sized FROM a ___", which wants a quantity - you size from a number, not from a proposition. Second, and decisively, the stem asks for the MOST PRECISE word, and "assumption" names the propositional attitude while "estimate" names the thing the pattern is actually cut to. Genuinely hard, correctly labelled; a strong student will spend time here, which is where the time belongs. FOUR-WORDS-AFTER TEST: CLEAN. The blank is sentence-final ("sized from a guess."), so there are no words after it at all within the sentence; every clue is in the two FOLLOWING sentences and must be read as prose. That is the right construction, though note it is clean by a different mechanism from Q06 - forward-reading rather than back-reading - so the two together give the passage a healthy mix. Minor interaction to be aware of: this item and Q10 both operate on paragraph 5, and Q10's inserted sentence would sit immediately before the sentence this blank lives in. Placement does not change the answer here, but a student who works Q10 first sees a slightly different paragraph.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q10.note: The added sentence states the general condition the whole paragraph then answers - some metals arrive with no published figure - so it belongs in front of the paragraph's first specific instance, the new alloy sized from a guess. General premise, then case: Point [A]. [C] would cut the two-step procedure (cuts and waits / measures cold) in half. [D] is redundant on arrival, since the closing sentence already says "a silicon bronze nobody upstate had a figure for". THE COMPETITOR IS [B], and it deserves stating because it is not weak: placed there, the sentence explains retroactively why a guess was needed and sits directly in front of "the published figure", giving that definite phrase a neat antecedent. I vote exclusive against it on sequence - at [B] the sentence raises a problem the paragraph has already announced and begun solving one sentence earlier, and it interrupts guess-then-how-she-guesses; a premise that motivates the opening sentence cannot sit after the opening sentence. Re-rated medium against the batch's hard: the sentence is a textbook paragraph-opening generalisation and [C]/[D] fall away quickly, so the real work is a single [A]-versus-[B] judgement. Not a Conventions or Knowledge-of-Language item, so the four-words-after shortcut does not apply; the analogous blind check is more reassuring than Q04's - the four options here are bare position labels carrying no propositional content of their own, so a blind solver has nothing to rank and must fall back on positional priors.
